l3.why: New data on topical roflumilast (cream or foam): case reports in new indications (lichen sclerosus, bullous pemphigoid, Darier, morphea, scarring alopecia), real-world and combination use, safety and pharmacovigilance, meta-analyses. Every one led its email; case reports go into the case report bibliography.

l3.intent: Roflumilast discussed in a broader article
l3.why: Reviews, consensus papers and comparisons whose abstract discusses roflumilast. The reviewer quotes how roflumilast is positioned next to competitors, including statements to correct.

Network meta-analyses, indirect comparisons and side-by-side safety reviews that rank roflumilast against tapinarof, ruxolitinib, delgocitinib or crisaborole. These need a response (the scalp NMA and the pediatric NMA were sent to Brett for comment).

Guidelines, expert consensus, Delphi panels and position statements decide where topicals sit in the treatment algorithm (AAD pediatric AD guideline, NPF severity definitions, CHE and topical non-steroidal consensus, AhR consensus, genital psoriasis Delphi).

New adverse-event reports for competing topicals (tapinarof folliculitis, comedones and contact allergy; ruxolitinib eczema herpeticum; FAERS analyses; maximal-use exposure). Used in safety and differentiation conversations.

Evidence of harm from topical corticosteroids: Cushing syndrome and HPA suppression in infants, type 2 diabetes risk, central serous retinopathy, raised eye pressure, barrier damage, allergens in formulations, tinea incognito. Supports non-steroidal first-line and maintenance use.

Reviews, case series and diagnostic work on topical steroid withdrawal. The reviewer sent the treatment update, the NIH 'dissecting the controversy' review and the updated systematic review; they serve as references for TSW conversations.

l3.intent: Topical steroid use patterns and stewardship
l3.why: How TCS are actually prescribed (potency escalation, quantities, response definitions, primary-care management). Context for where non-steroidals fit and for education programs.

l3.intent: Seborrheic dermatitis: disease and treatment paradigm
l3.why: Roflumilast foam is approved for seborrheic dermatitis. Almost every SD article was sent: burden and psychiatric comorbidity, diagnostic criteria, mechanisms, antifungal stewardship, consensus, pipeline.

l3.intent: PDE4 inhibitor class: mechanism and pipeline
l3.why: PDE4 inhibition in skin (mechanism beyond inflammation, orismilast chemistry, oral roflumilast in AD, the PDE4 landscape, apremilast combinations). It is roflumilast's class.

l3.intent: Topicals combined with systemic, biologic or device therapy
l3.why: Adding a topical non-steroidal to a biologic, oral therapy or laser/phototherapy for residual disease (tapinarof added to biologics, roflumilast on dupilumab, tapinarof with apremilast or NB-UVB).
Reviews of the topical options. The reviewer reads them for how roflumilast is described next to competitors and quotes the lines that help or hurt it.

Trials, long-term extensions, pooled analyses and real-world studies of tapinarof, topical ruxolitinib and delgocitinib (TRuE-AD4, DELTA TEEN, delgocitinib in AD, tapinarof in Japanese children, ruxolitinib claims analyses).
Claims, Medicare/Medicaid, payer and cost analyses of topicals and AD care (ruxolitinib Part D growth, insurance type and non-steroidal use, budget impact, pediatric pharmacy costs).
Vehicles, excipients and contact allergens in topicals (parabens in roflumilast cream, allergens in TCS formulations, tapinarof as a contact allergen, vehicle formulation of non-steroidal creams).
Infection, cardiovascular and malignancy risk across JAK inhibitors, including how topical exposure is separated from oral (boxed-warning context for topical ruxolitinib and delgocitinib).
Genital, intertriginous, scalp, face, nail and palmoplantar disease and severity definitions that count these sites. Roflumilast is labelled for intertriginous use, so special-site data matters.
Children and infants with AD or psoriasis treated topically (guidelines, treatment patterns, emerging topicals). Roflumilast is approved down to age 2 with trials from 3 months.
Quality of life, psychiatric comorbidity, itch and sleep burden, adherence, patient preferences and uncontrolled disease. Supports unmet-need and patient-centred messaging.

l3.intent: Off-label use of topical non-steroidals (case reports)
l3.why: Case reports and series of tapinarof, topical ruxolitinib or delgocitinib in other diseases (lichen planus, Hailey-Hailey, rosacea, lichen sclerosus, Darier). Usually listed as FYI; shows where competitors are expanding.
Chronic hand eczema treatment and burden. Delgocitinib is approved here, so it is a competitive space.
Use of topicals in pregnancy and the postpartum period (lack of human data for roflumilast and tapinarof).
Investigational agents and early-phase programs (rosacea and HS pipelines that include roflumilast, TAP-1502, new topical classes).
Meeting abstracts were never sent; posters reach the team through congress coverage.
INTEGUMENT, DERMIS, ARRECTOR and STRATUM papers and their plain-language summaries are Arcutis's own publications, known to the team before they appear; none were sent.

Posters, encore abstracts and analyses funded by Arcutis or written by its employees reach the team internally; none was sent, while independent roflumilast reports always were. Arcutis-supported expert consensus papers are the exception (the genital psoriasis Delphi was sent with congratulations).

l3.intent: Oral/systemic JAK inhibitor or non-dermatology JAK use
l3.why: Oral JAK inhibitor studies (alopecia areata, vitiligo, lupus, dermatomyositis, GVHD, myelofibrosis) dominate the ruxolitinib and topical-JAK terms but were not sent unless a topical was the subject.

l3.intent: Vitiligo or alopecia areata (no Arcutis indication)
l3.why: Ruxolitinib-in-vitiligo and JAK-in-alopecia-areata papers were not sent; roflumilast in vitiligo was.
Animal, cell and drug-delivery studies were rarely sent (two exceptions, both PDE4/tapinarof chemistry).
